opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most direct way into it is through von Neumann. In the late 1940s, before anybody knew what DNA did, von Neumann was thinking about what it would take for a machine to reproduce itself, a robot paddling around in a pond full of parts and assembling a copy of itself. He realized that to do it, the machine needs a set of instructions, a tape. It needs a constructor that can read the tape and build whatever the tape describes. And it needs a way to copy the tape and hand the copy to the offspring. And then he noticed something remarkable: the constructor that reads instructions and acts on them is a universal Turing machine. It's a computer. So the ability to reproduce, which is about as basic a property of life as you can name, requires computation. Not as a metaphor, but literally.

A few years later Watson and Crick, building on Rosalind Franklin's work, found that this is exactly how biology does it. DNA is the tape, the ribosome is the universal constructor, and polymerases copy the tape. Von Neumann predicted the architecture of the cell from first principles.

So when I say life is computational, I mean that living things are, in a very precise sense, computers that compute themselves. They take in matter and energy and use information processing to build and maintain and copy their own structure. That's what lets them persist against the second law of thermodynamics. A rock just sits there and erodes. A living thing actively keeps reconstructing itself, and that reconstruction is a computation.

There's also an empirical side I find compelling. We ran experiments with very simple artificial worlds, basically a minimal programming language with random strings of code interacting. You start with noise, with no replicators at all, and after a few million interactions, self-replicating programs spontaneously appear and take over. So computation isn't just compatible with life. When you have a substrate that can compute, life seems to be what tends to happen.

And once you see it that way, a lot follows. Symbiogenesis, the way life's complexity increases largely through mergers, things like mitochondria joining with cells, looks a lot like computational systems composing into larger ones. And intelligence starts to look less like a separate phenomenon and more like a continuation of the same story. Brains, and arguably what we're building now with AI, are life's computational nature turned toward modeling the world and modeling one another.

r005.rationale: The response describes copying the tape to offspring but does not explain that changes to genetic instructions can be inherited.

r006.rationale: It states that reproduction requires computation and maps the cell’s constructor to a universal Turing machine, a computer.

r007.rationale: It explicitly says DNA is the biological tape in this computational architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that life is, at bottom, something that makes copies of itself, and copying is a computational act. If you look at what a cell actually does, it's running a kind of program. DNA is a symbolic code, it gets transcribed, it gets interpreted, the machinery that does the interpreting is itself specified by the code. That's not a metaphor. That's literally the architecture of a self-replicating program, the kind of thing von Neumann worked out on paper in the 1940s before anyone knew what DNA looked like. He reasoned that a self-reproducing automaton needs a description of itself, a constructor that reads the description, and a mechanism to copy the description. A few years later, Watson and Crick found exactly that structure sitting in every cell.

And there's a deeper point, which is that computation isn't something humans invented and then noticed in biology. It's the other way around. Turing's insight was that there's a universal kind of machine, and universality means that once you cross a certain threshold of complexity, you can compute anything. What I find striking is that life seems to have found that threshold on its own, and I'd argue it's the thing that explains why evolution goes anywhere interesting at all. Natural selection by itself just filters. It doesn't tell you where the open-endedness comes from. But if what's being selected are programs, and programs can combine with other programs, can symbiose, can be composed into larger functional wholes, then you get this ratchet toward complexity that looks a lot like what we actually see across the history of life.

We've actually been running experiments on this. If you take a soup of random bits of code, really minimal instruction sets, no fitness function, nothing you'd call a reward, and just let them interact with each other and occasionally mutate, self-replicators spontaneously emerge. And then they start forming more complex structures, getting more complicated over time. Nobody told them to. That tells me that the emergence of life-like dynamics is something computation does when you let it, rather than something improbable that needed a miracle.

So when I say life is computational, I don't mean that life is like a computer in the way your laptop is a computer. I mean that computation is the right level of description for what life is. Matter is the substrate, physics is the substrate, but the thing that persists, the thing that evolves, the thing that gets passed down, is information and the functions that act on it. And once you take that seriously, a lot of the hard boundaries we like to draw, between living and nonliving, between brains and minds, between natural and artificial intelligence, start to look a lot more like differences of degree than differences of kind.

r001.rationale: It says the machinery that interprets DNA is itself specified by the code, matching the requirement that instructions describe their interpreter.

r002.rationale: It says von Neumann worked out self-reproduction on paper in the 1940s, before Watson and Crick found the corresponding structure in cells.

r003.rationale: It mentions a constructor in von Neumann’s architecture but does not identify ribosomes as its biological counterpart.

r004.rationale: It mentions a mechanism for copying the description but does not identify DNA polymerase as the instruction-tape copier.

r005.rationale: It discusses copying and mutation, but does not state that copying genetic instructions lets changes in them be inherited by offspring.

r006.rationale: It describes cells as running programs and discusses universal machines, but does not state that cellular reproduction requires a universal computer inside the cell.

r007.rationale: It calls DNA a symbolic code, but does not identify DNA as a literal instance of a Turing tape.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by computation. I don’t mean that an organism is a laptop, or that the universe is literally running on somebody’s computer. I mean that living systems process information, and that this processing is central to how they persist, reproduce, and evolve.

Think about a bacterium moving along a chemical gradient. It has to sense something about its environment, respond to that signal, and regulate its own activity. There’s a continuous loop between the organism and the world. The computation isn’t separate from the chemistry; it’s something the chemistry does.

Reproduction brings another aspect into focus. Genetic information can be copied, varied, and expressed in ways that help construct another organism. Those variations then have consequences for whether reproduction continues. So you have information that participates in making the machinery that carries and copies it.

That’s why I find the computational perspective useful. It connects the molecular processes inside an organism with behavior and evolution. But it has to be an embodied understanding of computation: one that involves matter, energy, and an environment. An abstract program doesn’t have to keep itself alive. An organism does.

r005.rationale: It mentions genetic information being copied and varied, but does not clearly state that changes are inherited by offspring.

r006.rationale: It describes information processing in living systems but does not state that cellular reproduction requires a universal computer.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to clarify is what we mean by computation. I don’t mean that a cell is a little laptop, or that the universe is running a program somewhere. I mean that living systems process information, and that processing is central to what makes them alive.

Think about a bacterium moving up a nutrient gradient. It has to sense something about its environment, retain information over time, and use that information to change what it does. That’s a computation, even though it’s implemented chemically rather than with silicon transistors.

And that goes all the way down. DNA is information, but it doesn’t do anything in isolation. You need the machinery of the cell to interpret it, regulate it, copy it, and turn it into action. The organism is this ongoing process of maintaining itself through exchanges of matter, energy, and information.

What I find especially interesting is that evolution changes the information processing itself. Living things don’t just execute a fixed set of instructions; over generations, they develop new ways of sensing, acting, and interacting. So computation gives us a language for connecting molecular biology to behavior and, eventually, cognition. It doesn’t replace chemistry or physics. It helps explain how those physical processes become organized into something that can keep itself alive.
